strengths: Originality/significance: IMPspec offers a novel spectral construction for uncertainty over RKHS-represented interventional functions. Expanding the function class and placing GP priors on Mercer coordinates is an interesting way to avoid the bespoke nuclear-dominant kernels used by BayesIMP.

Soundness: The paper derives closed-form posterior first and second moments and shows that the posterior mean coincides with an established kernel-ridge causal estimator. The analysis of BayesIMP’s tail collapse provides useful theoretical insight beyond proposing a new method.

Evidence: Across the toy and synthetic experiments, IMPspec has competitive point-estimation error and substantially better reported in- and out-of-distribution calibration. The causal Bayesian optimization experiments also suggest that the uncertainty estimates can improve downstream decisions.

Presentation: The main construction is motivated clearly, notation is generally organized, and the appendix supplies extensive derivations, data-generating mechanisms, identification arguments, algorithms, and baseline details.

Ethics: The experiments do not expose patients to interventions, and the paper appropriately notes the potential cost of exploratory medical interventions and the motivation for reducing their number.
weaknesses: Soundness: Algorithm 2 is incorrect as written. It tests each bootstrap posterior mean against the interval returned by Algorithm 1 for that same bootstrap sample; because that interval is centered on that mean, the indicator is identically one and the calibration objective cannot distinguish spectral measures. The appendix describes a materially different 50:50 sample-split procedure, but the central algorithm and its inputs do not express it.

Soundness: The claimed consistency result for calibration does not convincingly repair this issue. Theorem 6 mixes the sampling law, bootstrap law, and an independently fitted plug-in estimator; several distributional objects in the proof are ill-defined or compared without applying a common statistic. The displayed Kolmogorov-distance argument therefore does not establish consistency of the implemented calibration loss.

Uncertainty claims are overstated: the reported intervals are central intervals of a moment-matched Gaussian approximation, not credible intervals containing the stated mass under the actual non-Gaussian IMPspec posterior. No approximation-error analysis or comparison with posterior sampling is provided.

Evidence/significance: The evaluation consists of two small synthetic settings and a healthcare simulator, not an application to observed healthcare outcomes. The broad claims of state-of-the-art causal uncertainty quantification are therefore insufficiently supported, particularly for higher-dimensional covariates, larger samples, non-Gaussian outcomes, kernel misspecification, or violations of causal identification assumptions.

Reproducibility: The manuscript says “Code can be found at” but supplies no URL. Although many experimental settings are documented, the discrepancy between Algorithm 2 and the appendix implementation, unspecified optimization details such as initialization and constraints, and modifications made to the BayesIMP baseline impede faithful reproduction.

Presentation/limitations: There is no focused limitations discussion. Important limitations—including cubic GP scaling, reliance on Gaussian surrogate likelihoods, moment-matching error, sensitivity to kernels and the spectral-measure family, and the strong causal graph/identification assumptions—are not adequately analyzed. The healthcare framing should also distinguish more clearly between a simulator informed by published statistics and validation on real patient-level data.

strengths: Originality: The spectral construction is an interesting way to place tractable priors on RKHS-valued conditional mean embeddings, while retaining the kernel-ridge causal estimator as the posterior mean. The closed-form posterior moments and weighted spectral training objective are potentially useful contributions. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_icml2026_tianyi_medium_20260920T0418Z/scratch/186734f4b1474dc99834bc34bf9cf082/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Significance: Uncertainty quantification for continuous-treatment causal functions is important, and avoiding unstable propensity weighting is practically appealing. The framework covers several estimands and both single-dataset and data-fusion settings.
Presentation: The main conceptual progression is generally clear, and the extensive appendix supplies assumptions, derivations, implementation details, and analyses of two pathologies in BayesIMP.
Evaluation: The paper reports 50-trial experiments, in- and out-of-distribution calibration, comparisons with several baselines, ablations, and downstream causal Bayesian optimization results.

Ethics: The experiments appear simulation-based, so there are no evident privacy or human-subject concerns; the paper also briefly recognizes the cost and risk of exploratory healthcare interventions.
weaknesses: Soundness—probabilistic model: Equation (11) simultaneously treats every Mercer coordinate of the same observed V as an independent Gaussian regression observation, φ_i(V)=μ_i(Z)+ξ_i. These coordinates are deterministic, mutually constrained transforms of one V and generally cannot have the proposed conditionally independent Gaussian joint distribution. This is especially clear on compact domains, where continuous eigenfunctions are bounded whereas additive Gaussian observations have unbounded support. Calling the construction a surrogate does not repair the absence of a coherent likelihood or justify ordinary Bayesian posterior-coverage claims.

Soundness—posterior proof: The factorization used to derive Theorem 1 depends directly on that questionable model. The proof additionally claims that an atomless conditional law of V has a Lebesgue density; this is false, and V is allowed to be an arbitrary standard Borel variable for which Lebesgue measure may not even be defined. Consequently, the claimed posterior independence and coordinate-wise factorization are not established.

Soundness—calibration algorithm: Algorithm 2 tests whether the bootstrap posterior mean μ̂^(b) lies in the credible interval CI^(b) computed around that same mean. For every nondegenerate central interval this indicator is identically one, making the stated loss independent of the spectral parameter except through numerical pathologies. The appendix describes sample splitting but does not give an unambiguous corrected algorithm, so the reported calibration improvements cannot be reproduced from the manuscript. The later consistency result does not resolve this discrepancy.

Evidence: The moment-matched Gaussian is treated as providing credible intervals although the true posterior is explicitly non-Gaussian and heavy-tailed. There is no experiment measuring the accuracy of this Gaussian approximation, and the claimed process-level KL projection is not rigorously justified. Thus accurate variances alone would not support the interval claims.

Evaluation: Evidence is limited to two small synthetic setups and a healthcare simulator assembled from published equations; this is not a real healthcare-data application as the main text suggests. Several differences are modest relative to trial variability, no paired significance analysis is given, calibration is estimated from only 50 trials, and IMPspec receives an explicit calibration-tuning procedure that is not comparably applied to baselines.

The Bayesian-optimization study adds an RBF covariance to every causal surrogate, but does not isolate how much improvement comes from the proposed covariance rather than the inherited kernel estimator, added RBF kernel, or hyperparameter choices. Only ten iterations and three closely related simulated tasks are evaluated.

Reproducibility and presentation: The sentence “Code can be found at” has no URL. There are broken references to a nonexistent Section D.2, notation and equation inconsistencies, and missing details such as optimization domains and initialization. These issues are material given the mismatch between Algorithm 2 and the reported implementation.

Limitations and ethics: The paper thoroughly criticizes BayesIMP but does not comparably discuss its own misspecification, cubic scaling, bootstrap cost, sensitivity to kernel and spectral choices, overlap assumptions, or risks of using observationally derived uncertainty for treatment optimization. The brief healthcare warning does not address how erroneous uncertainty estimates could affect deployment.

Overall: The spectral idea has merit and the presentation is ambitious, but the incoherent coordinate likelihood and apparently degenerate calibration algorithm undermine the central posterior and calibration claims. These are acceptance-blocking technical and reproducibility problems, warranting a score of 2 rather than a borderline recommendation.

strengths: The manuscript presents a technically interesting and original construction for uncertainty over continuous-treatment causal functions. Expanding the function class and using a spectral representation produces closed-form posterior moments while preserving the established kernel estimator of Singh et al. as the posterior mean. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_icml2026_tianyi_medium_20260920T0418Z/scratch/c757e8e6800d49208c37a25704bd8ae3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The paper provides substantial mathematical development: it states topological and kernel assumptions, proves the interventional-process representation, derives posterior moments and extensions to incremental and average effects, and analyzes failure modes of BayesIMP.

The empirical results are consistently favorable. Across 50-trial experiments, IMPspec improves both point estimation and calibration, with especially strong out-of-distribution calibration relative to BayesIMP (0.108 versus 0.485 error in Table 2). The ablations also show that spectral calibration improves coverage.

The contribution is potentially significant: reliable uncertainty for nonparametric continuous-treatment effects is important, and the causal Bayesian-optimization experiments illustrate a useful downstream role for the inferred covariance rather than evaluating uncertainty in isolation.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The causal estimands, variable mappings, algorithms, data-generating processes, and baseline implementations are described in considerable detail, and the figures effectively expose underfitting and variance-collapse behavior in prior work.

The work uses synthetic or simulator-based data rather than intervening on patients, and I found no material research-ethics concern. The warning that exploratory medical interventions can be costly is appropriate.
weaknesses: The central Bayesian construction has an unresolved coherence issue. Equation (11) treats every Mercer coordinate phi_i(V) as an independently Gaussian-noisy observation with common variance, even though the infinite coordinate sequence must correspond to a single V and is constrained to the image of the feature map. The posterior-factorization proof then invokes a joint likelihood/density for V from these infinitely many coordinate models. Injectivity does not establish that the independent-coordinate Gaussian model induces a probability distribution on V, and the claim that V has a Lebesgue density is not meaningful for the stated general standard-Borel spaces. Calling this a probabilistic surrogate does not by itself justify the exact-posterior and KL-projection claims. A coherent Hilbert-valued observation model, finite-truncation limit, or generalized-Bayes formulation is needed.

The calibration theory is weaker than the framing suggests. Theorem 6 assumes bootstrap consistency rather than establishing it for this estimator, requires sample splitting and additional smoothness, and bounds a plug-in cumulative probability at a fixed point; it does not directly prove uniform calibration of Algorithm 2 after selecting the spectral parameter over grids. Thus the method is empirically calibrated, but broad claims of principled calibrated credible intervals should be qualified.

The evaluation is narrow for a state-of-the-art claim: causal-effect uncertainty is tested on only two small synthetic designs (primarily n=100), while the healthcare result is a simulator assembled from a published linear association with R-squared 0.13, not validation on real patient-level causal outcomes. The latter should be described consistently as semi-synthetic rather than a healthcare application.

Scalability is not demonstrated. Training is cubic in n, spectral covariance estimation is said to use potentially far more than one million Monte Carlo samples, and there are no runtime, memory, Monte Carlo sensitivity, or larger-sample experiments.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the main text says “Code can be found at” but supplies no repository, and several appendix cross-references point to nonexistent Section D.2. Important numerical details such as search domains for Bayesian optimization and the final Monte Carlo sample count for IMPspec are also not fully specified.

Some mathematical statements require correction. Proposition 2 assumes log-convex h but its proof uses the log-concave inequality; the subsequent remark incorrectly lists the Gaussian kernel as log-convex. There are also covariance/notation inconsistencies in the appendix, including the definition of k-hat(z,z') and the average-effect corollary.

The limitations discussion focuses mostly on BayesIMP rather than IMPspec. It should explicitly discuss likelihood misspecification, sensitivity to causal identification and kernel choices, computational scaling, extrapolation risk, and the limited evidential value of the healthcare simulator. These issues presently outweigh the promising conceptual and empirical merits.

strengths: Originality: The spectral-coordinate construction is a creative way to combine conditional mean embeddings with standard GP regression while preserving the kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024) as the posterior mean.

Significance: Uncertainty quantification for continuous-treatment and conditional causal functions is important, and the proposed closed-form moment calculations could be practically useful if placed on a sound probabilistic or generalized-Bayes foundation.

Soundness strengths: The manuscript derives explicit posterior mean, variance, and cross-covariance formulas, carefully treats the unbounded isonormal process representation, and analyzes two concrete pathologies of BayesIMP. The synthetic experiments include calibration error, proper interval scores, heavy-tailed noise, limited support, and calibration ablations.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished. The appendices provide detailed data-generating processes, baseline configurations, hyperparameters, and derivations.

Limitations and ethics: The paper openly acknowledges surrogate-likelihood and Gaussian-approximation limitations, states the dependence on causal identification assumptions, and appropriately warns against unvalidated high-stakes use.
weaknesses: Soundness—central probabilistic model: Equation (11) is not shown to define a coherent joint likelihood for V. It assigns independent Gaussian noise to every Mercer coordinate phi_i(V), although all coordinates arise from the same V and must lie in the highly constrained image of the feature map. For common continuous V, an infinite independently perturbed coordinate vector will almost surely not correspond to any V. The proof of Theorem 4.1 nevertheless invokes a density p(V | (mu_i),Z), factorization across coordinates, and Bayes' rule. The appendix's argument that atomless coordinates imply a Lebesgue density for V is false, especially under the stated general standard-Borel spaces. The resulting construction may be interpretable as a modular or generalized posterior, but it is not the Bayesian posterior claimed in the paper.

Soundness—calibration target: Algorithm 2 calibrates whether an independently estimated, noisy plug-in value lies in bootstrap intervals, rather than whether the fixed true causal effect lies in them. With a 50/50 split, plug-in error is generally of the same order as interval width, so this targets the distribution of the difference between two estimators and can inflate intervals. Mere consistency of the plug-in estimator is insufficient; its error must be negligible relative to interval width or explicitly corrected.

Soundness—theoretical calibration result: Theorem C.9 does not resolve this problem. Its proof uses a Lipschitz constant for a sample-size-dependent distribution without controlling that constant, conflates bootstrap/sample or statistic distributions in the Kolmogorov term, and contains unclear or invalid transformations involving the random interval boundary. Ordinary bootstrap consistency also requires centering, scaling, and regularity that are not established here. Thus the claimed calibration consistency and argmin guarantee are unsupported.

The likelihood-ratio analysis in Section A.4 assumes an unspecified well-specified benchmark likelihood and an unverified chi-squared moment bound. It is a generic conditional perturbation statement, not evidence that the proposed surrogate posterior is close to a valid causal posterior.

The paper motivates uncertainty for an entire causal function, but reports and calibrates pointwise intervals averaged over grids. It provides neither simultaneous-band coverage nor a guarantee for the whole function, so the framing is broader than the demonstrated result.

Evaluation is encouraging but too narrow to overcome the foundational issues: uncertainty coverage is tested on only two main synthetic designs at n=100, using 50 trials, and the real 401(k) example has no ground truth. The real-data claim that the 95% band excludes zero therefore cannot validate coverage, and the chosen adjustment set and unconfoundedness assumption are not substantively justified.

Reproducibility is mixed. The extensive implementation details are helpful, but no code or artifact availability is stated, several custom baseline modifications are required, and the reported calibration runtime is surprisingly insensitive to 10 versus 100 bootstrap replications. Randomness and optimization details are not fully specified across experiments.

Presentation is strong overall, but consequential notation and proof issues remain—for example, variance versus standard deviation is ambiguous in the calibration theorem, some covariance expressions use inconsistent arguments, and the manuscript repeatedly calls pseudo-intervals posterior credible intervals despite the unresolved likelihood coherence problem. These issues prevent others from reliably building on the central UQ claim.

strengths: Original and technically interesting construction: the spectral representation permits standard GP priors and yields closed-form posterior moments, while the posterior mean exactly recovers the established kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024).

The manuscript is clearly organized and unusually transparent about using a surrogate coordinate-wise Gaussian likelihood and a moment-matched Gaussian approximation rather than exact posterior inference.

The synthetic studies report repeated trials, coverage across many nominal levels, interval scores, robustness checks, and several useful ablations. The causal Bayesian optimization experiments also illustrate a plausible downstream use.

Implementation details are extensive, and the limitations and impact discussions appropriately acknowledge dependence on identification assumptions and the risks of misleading uncertainty in high-stakes applications.
weaknesses: Soundness is the decisive concern. Algorithm 1 does not produce credible intervals for the actual non-Gaussian interventional-process posterior; it produces Gaussian intervals after moment matching. The surrogate likelihood in Eq. (11) additionally treats infinitely many spectral coordinates through a highly misspecified coordinate-wise Gaussian model. Thus, the central uncertainty claim rests on two uncontrolled approximations.

Appendix A.4 does not substantively control this approximation error. It assumes an abstract likelihood-ratio moment bound involving an unspecified well-specified likelihood, without showing that the proposed surrogate satisfies the bound or estimating its magnitude. The remaining error from Gaussian moment matching is merely left as an unknown total-variation term.

The calibration theory is conditional on consistency of both the bootstrap and plug-in estimator. These properties are not established for the proposed function-valued procedure, weak-overlap regimes, or the actual hyperparameter-fitting pipeline. Theorem C.9 therefore does not establish valid coverage for the reported intervals, and finite-sample calibration relies on treating a noisy split-sample estimate as ground truth.

The main empirical comparison confounds posterior quality with method-specific calibration: IMPspec is bootstrap-calibrated, whereas the competing GP posteriors are not given an analogous generic scale-calibration procedure. Since calibration changes IMPspec's error from 0.10 to 0.07 in Table 1, a calibrated-baseline comparison is necessary to attribute the gain to the proposed construction.

Evidence is narrow relative to the broad uncertainty-quantification claims: coverage is validated on only two synthetic data-generating processes, both with n=100 and closely related kernel-GP baselines. The 401(k) study has no ground truth and consequently cannot validate coverage; nevertheless, the paper interprets exclusion of zero as evidence of a positive causal effect without sensitivity analysis for confounding, overlap, or identification.

Some comparisons have limited diagnostic value. ORF is knowingly misspecified as linear in treatment, Continuous DR is given data from a fixed-B conditional subproblem rather than the common observational sample, and the strongest BayesIMP configuration appears only in an appendix ablation. These choices do not establish superiority over well-tuned modern alternatives.

Reproducibility is incomplete: despite many implementation details, the manuscript provides no code or repository, only one explicit random seed for the real-data preprocessing, and insufficient information about optimization stability and trial seeds. Reproducing the bespoke BayesIMP modifications and full bootstrap-calibration pipeline would be difficult.

The limitations discussion is honest but understates the central issue: richer approximations are presented as future improvement, whereas the current paper lacks evidence that its nominal posterior intervals have a reliable inferential interpretation beyond the studied simulations. These weaknesses outweigh the originality and good presentation.

strengths: [Originality/significance] IMPSPEC offers a useful new synthesis: spectral representations permit standard GP priors for RKHS-based interventional functions, while the posterior mean exactly recovers the established kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024). This is a meaningful contribution for uncertainty quantification of function-valued causal effects. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_icml2026_tianyi_medium_20260920T0418Z/scratch/012d40b1504741bf8049bec18894b66e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

[Soundness] The paper derives closed-form posterior moments, treats incremental and averaged effects, proves the posterior-mean/KRR equivalence, and carefully justifies the interchange involving the unbounded isonormal process. The analysis of BayesIMP's nonstationarity and out-of-support variance collapse is technically informative.

[Evidence] Across the toy and benchmark simulations, IMPSPEC has the best reported calibration error and interval score, while retaining competitive or superior RMSE. Ablations cover spectral calibration, sample splitting, kernel choice, bootstrap count, heavy-tailed noise, and limited treatment support.
[Usefulness] The causal Bayesian optimization experiments demonstrate a concrete downstream benefit: lower cumulative regret across front-door, back-door, and healthcare-simulator tasks.

[Presentation/reproducibility] The manuscript is clear and professionally presented. Its extensive appendix specifies data-generating processes, estimands, algorithms, hyperparameters, baselines, metrics, runtime, and memory, making the experiments substantially reproducible from the description.

[Limitations/ethics] The authors appropriately disclose the surrogate likelihood, Gaussian moment-matching approximation, scalability limitation, dependence on identification assumptions, and risks of misplaced confidence in high-stakes applications.
weaknesses: [Soundness] The claimed uncertainty quality is primarily empirical. The intervals arise from a misspecified coordinate-wise Gaussian surrogate followed by a moment-matched Gaussian approximation; the likelihood-ratio analysis only gives conditional bounds under an assumed moment-control condition and does not show that this condition holds for the proposed model.

[Calibration theory] The calibration-consistency result is conditional on consistency of the empirical bootstrap distribution and plug-in estimator. It therefore does not itself establish nominal frequentist coverage for the causal function under concrete, verifiable assumptions. Finite-sample validity—the practical motivation of calibration—remains heuristic.

[Evaluation breadth] UQ accuracy is established on only two principal synthetic designs with 50 trials. The 401(k) study has no ground truth or comparator, so its credible bands demonstrate feasibility rather than calibration or causal validity. Broader benchmark families and sensitivity to overlap, dimension, sample size, and causal-model misspecification would make the evidence more convincing.

[Comparators] Some frequentist baselines are structurally mismatched to the nonlinear conditional target, while the closest Bayesian comparison is mainly BayesIMP. Comparisons against additional modern continuous-treatment or Bayesian CATE uncertainty methods would better isolate the contribution.

[Statistical evidence] Several numerical differences in RMSE and causal Bayesian optimization are modest relative to their reported variation, but the paper does not provide paired uncertainty estimates or hypothesis tests supporting claims such as significantly improved performance.

[Reproducibility/scalability] No code or artifact link is provided. Moreover, nominal inference remains cubic in sample size and requires Monte Carlo approximation with up to 10^5–10^6 spectral samples; minibatch marginal-likelihood optimization is an engineering workaround rather than a demonstrated scalable GP approximation.
